newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S. pounded by freezing rain, snow.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S. pounded by freezing rain, snow.

text.p: Snow and freezing rain pounded the Western United States on Thursday, ruining the holiday travel plans of thousands in Oregon and causing traffic tie-ups from northern California to Washington.

The icy weather caused a major power outage at Portland International Airport, forcing flight delays and cancellations that stranded travelers for hours. The power was restored later, but flights remained behind schedule.
"We're through the worst of it," Portland airport spokesman Darrel Buttice said. "It (the outage) caused cancellation of flights and delays on certainly one of the busiest days of the year."

Four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) of fresh snow fell in the Seattle area, causing traffic accidents and other problems for holiday shoppers and travelers. Washington state officials warned that the storm would increase the likelihood of flooding.
"There has been a lot of rain and snow, a lot of accidents this morning on the highways," said Linda Ramsey, director of Washington state's emergency management division.

While Washington and Oregon took a beating, northern and central California saw moderate rain and snow at higher elevations. Major mountain highways in California and Nevada remained open despite several weather-related accidents.

But the National Weather Service issued a warning on Thursday that a second storm could hit California this weekend. The powerful Pacific storm was expected to reach the state's northern coast late on Friday or Saturday, bringing with it strong gusty winds, heavy rains as well as more snow.
The approaching storm, currently just north of the Hawaiian islands, could dump more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rain in some areas and cause flash flooding, forecasters said.
This weekend's storm "is looking to be a big one," National Weather Service forecaster Bob Diaz said. "There is the potential for flooding."
The storm could also wreak havoc on the Sierra Nevada, where residents are still digging out from the last pounding.

Last weekend, more than nine feet (3 metres) of snow fell in some parts of the popular Lake Tahoe ski resort area on the northern California-Nevada border. That blustery storm affected about 100,000 Pacific Gas & Electric Co. customers in the Sierras. Power has been restored to nearly everyone.
PG&E said it was preparing for the incoming storm.
"We're always keeping one eye on the weather and taking the steps that have to be taken in advance," PG&E spokesman Leonard Anderson said.
